The maintenance window opened just after midnight and the release engineer
walked the checklist one line at a time. Nothing in the plan was clever. That
was deliberate. A deployment that depends on cleverness fails in a way nobody
can reason about at three in the morning, and the only thing worse than an
outage is an outage whose cause is a surprise to the people fixing it.

Each service drained its queue before it stopped accepting new work. The
drain took longer than expected on the reporting tier, which turned out to be
holding a batch of unacknowledged messages from an upstream that had itself
been restarted an hour earlier. The messages were not lost. They were simply
waiting, patiently and invisibly, for somebody to notice them.

We have learned to distrust the word simply. When a postmortem says a change
was simply a configuration update, it usually means nobody wrote down what the
old value was. The habit we try to build instead is boring and repetitive:
record the previous state, record the new state, record who decided and why,
and keep the record somewhere a stranger can find it without asking.

There is a temptation, once a system has run without incident for a season, to
believe the quiet is a property of the system rather than of the traffic. It
is almost never so. The quiet is usually a property of the load, and the load
changes when a customer changes, and customers change without warning us.

By four the window closed. The dashboards were green, the error budget had
barely moved, and the engineer wrote three sentences in the channel describing
what had happened and what had not. Those three sentences will be read by
somebody in eight months who has never met her, and they will save that person
an hour. That is the whole of the craft, most days: leaving a legible trail
behind ordinary work so the next person does not have to reconstruct it.

Nobody applauds a boring night. But a boring night is an achievement, and it
is bought with a hundred small refusals to take a shortcut that would have
worked this one time.
